title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up.

An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag.         September 9, 2026

            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feature the best battery life on iPhones to date.
                                            There's a new 5-minute fast wired charging feature which offers 50% battery life for just 15 minutes of charging time.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        While the iPhone 18 Pro looks similar to last year's model, the internals are a different story. The new A20 Pro processor with 32 Neural Engine cores will go a long way helping with on-device AI tasks—but you might not feel those differences all the time.The new updates to battery life and charging, however, will make an actual difference in daily use on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Apple is promising the best battery life on an iPhone yet, and is finally supporting faster wired charging.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Apple
                    
    
According to Apple, the regular sized iPhone 18 Pro will have the same battery life as the outgoing, larger iPhone 17 Pro Max model, which is quite a big deal. Apple is combining the efficiency gains in the A20 Pro chip with new battery technology to deliver this large leap in battery life. 
You will get 45 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and 36 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro model. The iPhone 18 Pro will last 24 hours per charge, while the 18 Pro Max can go up to 30 hours.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
According to Apple, this is based on tests performed with Apple's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with a 60W max charging speed. Wired fast charging is also supported with 60W-capable USB-C cables and USB PD 3.1 adapters that support Adjustable Voltage Supply.Faster wired charging finally comes to the iPhoneThe world of Android flagships is filled with quick-charging smartphones, and some of that clout will now come over to the iPhone as well. A quick five-minute wired charge will give you up to six hours of video playback, and more importantly, you get 50% charging in just 15 minutes. Even wireless charging is faster, with 50% charging in around 30 minutes.

title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

        At $154.99 for the Wi-Fi model, Apple’s refurbished 9th-generation iPad lands in the same price range as many budget Android tablets while still offering the polished experience people usually expect from an iPad. The Wi-Fi + Cellular version is probably the better value here since it costs only $15 more—and having built-in cellular connectivity means you are not constantly depending on public Wi-Fi or tethering from your phone, which makes a noticeable difference for commuters, students, rideshare drivers, and frequent travelers.And since Apple still supports this model with iPadOS 26 updates, you're not immediately stepping into outdated software either. That, combined with the “Grade A” refurbished condition (comes with little to no cosmetic wear) and included one-year warranty, still makes this older iPad a reasonable option for students, parents, travelers, or anyone looking for a dependable secondary device for reading, streaming, video calls, light work, and casual gaming. That said, it is not built for demanding creative workloads like professional video editing or heavy multitasking, but that limitation feels reasonable considering the price. The biggest compromise is the 64GB storage capacity, which works best for people who mostly stream content rather than store large games or video files locally.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
And while its A13 Bionic chip is older by Apple standards, it still keeps up with everyday use—apps launch quickly, Safari browsing stays smooth with multiple tabs open, and streaming services run without feeling sluggish. The 10.2-inch Retina display also holds up surprisingly well for everyday use, especially for reading articles and ebooks or watching videos. You still get Touch ID in the home button, stereo speakers, and support for the first-generation Apple Pencil for handwritten notes or sketching. Battery life also remains practical, with Apple estimating up to 10 hours of use on a charge, which is enough for a full day of browsing, streaming, and light work. All things considered, this 9th-gen iPad is a great deal.

title: Microsoft's Record-Setting Patch Tuesday Update Fixes Nearly 1,000 Flaws
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July.
                                            Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild.
                                            AI is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities as well as allowing developers to fix them more quickly.
                                            It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Security updates have been trending larger, and Microsoft's Patch Tuesday for September is no exception. The company just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July (the previous record). Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild. This massive jump is in large part due to AI, which is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities while also allowing developers to find and fix them more quickly. This means we're likely to continue seeing sizeable updates on shorter release cycles, ideally reducing the time hackers have to take advantage of these flaws. Microsoft has typically pushed Patch Tuesday fixes around 10 a.m. PT on the second Tuesday of every month. It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation. PC users should receive Patch Tuesday updates automatically, but you can check the status via Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates.
September's Patch Tuesday addresses 966 flaws with two zero-days As BleepingComputer reports, the 966 flaws fixed this month are broken down across the following categories: 438 elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, 19 security feature bypass vulnerabilities, 258 remote-code-execution vulnerabilities, 173 information disclosure vulnerabilities, 16 spoofing vulnerabilities, and 56 denial-of-service vulnerabilities. These figures do not include other vulnerabilities (204 in total across other Microsoft products) patched earlier this month. One of the zero-days addressed in September is an elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Windows Update Stack. CVE-2026-81963 allows attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges via improper link resolution before file access. The bug discovery has been attributed to Romain Deperne and the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Centre. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The other zero-day is also an elevation of privilege vulnerability. CVE-2026-85880 is a flaw in the Windows Advanced Local Procedure—an attacker could execute code in a low-privilege AppContainer, and the vulnerability could escape the sandbox and gain SYSTEM privileges locally. The bug was discovered by Volexity, as well as Mark Kelly, David Galazin, and Jeremy Hedges with Proofpoint. Both zero-days have been actively exploited in the wild, though Microsoft has not provided any details as to how.

title: A Bunch of AI Platforms Are Down, Including ChatGPT
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 3, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Robert Way via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.

            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple didn't mention the iPhone 18 as it launched the new Pro models.
                                            Most rumors point to a March 2027 launch for the standard iPhone 18.
                                            It should turn up alongside the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        There was something different about today's "Surprise and Shine" launch event from Apple: We didn't get the unveiling of the iPhone 18.For the first time since Apple started releasing multiple iPhones per year, which was 2013 with the arrival of the iPhone 5c and the iPhone 5s (simpler times), we have several pro-level handsets without the standard version to accompany them. So what's behind the shift? And is the iPhone 18 canceled? Apple, predictably, isn't saying, but we've got enough clues to make an informed guess.Why Apple didn't announce an iPhone 18
    
            
            The iPhone Duo was the star of today's show, as predicted.
                                        Credit: Apple
                    
    
If you've been keeping up with Apple rumors since the launch of the iPhone 17, you'll know that this has long been predicted—notably by the most respected purveyor of Apple leaks in the business, reporter Mark Gurman. Gurman was predicting in Bloomberg as far back as November 2025 that we would only get the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the folding iPhone Duo in 2026.
The reason? According to Gurman, it's to spread out revenue more evenly across the year, rather than having most of the iPhones unveiled every September. It also takes some of the pressure off Apple's marketing teams and reduces the likelihood of mishaps like that Siri AI upgrade—which was announced way before it was ready. Gurman also went on record as saying that this is likely to be the norm for "years to come," so get used to it.However, Gurman wasn't the first to break the news. In May of 2025, Wayne Ma at The Information reported that Apple would hold the standard iPhone 18 model over until 2027, based on conversations with anonymous supply chain sources. As per that report, one of the motivations behind the shift was to make more space for the folding iPhone, which makes sense considering it's Apple's first attempt at the form factor.Just a day later, well-known and usually well-informed Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo backed up the story, saying that we'd see the foldable iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Air 2 (then called the iPhone 18 Slim) in September 2026. Apart from that last handset, he was right.Kuo added an extra reason for the shift as well: Competition from phone manufacturers based in Asia. A lot of these manufacturers release their flagship handsets during the first half of the year, including Samsung, and as far as Apple is concerned, that can leave it playing catch-up by the time September rolls around.Here's when the iPhone 18 is expected to be announced
    
            
            The successor to the iPhone 17e should arrive with the iPhone 18.
                                        Credit: Apple
                    
    
While the iPhone 18 was a no-show at the "Surprise and Shine" event, there's no indication that it's been canceled. Apple still wants to cater to those who'd rather spend a little less on their iPhones (the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,119), and the most educated guesses we've seen suggest we'll get the base version of the phone sometime in March.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's unlikely to be on its own either. We're also expecting to see the iPhone 18e and the iPhone Air 2 appear at the same time, following on from the iPhone 17e (launched in March 2026) and the original iPhone Air (launched in September 2025, alongside the iPhone 17 series).And that "e" phone series set the foundation for the calendar shift we've now seen with the standard iPhone 18 model. The first of these more affordable handsets, the iPhone SE, showed up in March 2016—it was then followed by the iPhone SE 2 (April 2020), the iPhone SE 3 (March 2022), and the iPhone 16e (February 2025). That shows Apple has been eyeing up the February-March-April slot for non-pro-level iPhones for a decade at this point.The rumors so far suggest the iPhone 18 will use an A20 chipset, while we're likely to get a RAM bump as well. We now know that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have a smaller Dynamic Island, with the ability to show up to three Live Activities, and that's something that should carry across to the standard model (along with iOS 27).Apple didn't mention the iPhone 18 at all today—not even in a post-credits sequence—but it would be a major surprise if the handset didn't make a belated appearance sometime in the first quarter of next year. If this is the iPhone that's for you, you're just going to have to wait a little while longer.

title: Apple Just Announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple/YouTube
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple officially announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max on Wednesday.
                                            The new iPhones look like the previous generation, the iPhone 17 Pro, but have smaller Dynamic Islands and come in new colors.
                                            The iPhone 18 Pro series also comes with variable apertures for the first time on iPhone, which will improve light control and bokeh.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The iPhone Duo will inevitably steal tech headlines this week. After all, Apple finally made a foldable iPhone to compete with options from Samsung and Google. But while an iPhone with two displays is novel and exciting, it's also going to be expensive. I imagine there are many in the market for a new iPhone who aren't interested in spending as much as $2,000. There are also likely customers who don't want a foldable iPhone, and would prefer the standard smartphone design they're used to. That's where the iPhone 18 Pro comes in. iPhone 18 Pro: DesignIf you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you might confuse it for the iPhone 18 Pro. Indeed, Apple hasn't changed the overall design much this year, which is to be expected. The iPhone 17 Pro refreshed the Pro iPhone design with its large camera bump and plane of glass for MagSafe charging. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't much different—though now the metal is color-matched to the back glass.That being said, there are some changes here you may notice upon closer examination. Perhaps first you'd notice the 18 Pro's Dynamic Island is smaller than it has been on previous Pro iPhones. With it, you're able to run three tasks at once, rather than two. That may prove useful depending on what you're doing, or it may end up cluttering the top of your iPhone. 18 Pro users will have to be the judge. You'd also notice some new color options not available on the iPhone 17 Pro, which I'll cover below.    
The displays will remain the same sizes as last year—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro, and 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But now, these displays use a more efficient LPTO+ technology. iPhone 18 Pro: ProcessorLike the iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pros come with Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology. The company touts how the new chip is great for processing AI on-device, with a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, new Neural Accelerators, and a second Neural Engine. Apple focused on the A20 Pro's thermal cooling with the new vapor chamber in the 18 Pro. Apple says this means there are significant sustained performance improvements over the iPhone 17 Pro.    Apple says this chip has the fastest CPU in a smartphone, with 50% better memory bandwidth. But, as with all performance claims, we'll have to wait until testers try out the A20 Pro for themselves. Still, Apple's newest chips always improve on the previous generation by some degree, so it's safe to say the 18 Pro (and the Duo at that) will be the fastest iPhones yet. Apple also says the iPhone 18 Pro has 36 hours of battery life while streaming video, while iPhone 18 Pro Max has 45 hours. The company says five minutes of charging gets you six hours of video playback.   iPhone 18 Pro: CamerasPerhaps the biggest change for the iPhone 18 Pro this year is its cameras. Apple's Pro iPhones are known for their shooters, but for the 18 Pros, Apple has taken things up a notch. For the first time, these iPhones have variable apertures. When using the 48MP main camera, your iPhone can physically open and close its aperture to control how much light hits the sensor—up to 50% more light than before. That offers two benefits: In dim environments, you can let in more light than you normally could. You can also use the aperture to control the depth of field, or the background blur. A large aperture (more light) means a blurrier background, while a smaller aperture (less light) means a cleaner background. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple also introduced Pro Controls, which has been sorely missing on the iPhone. You now can control white balance and shutter speed, and check the histogram. This mode works for both photography and videography. There's now a new "smart focus tracking" feature that uses AI to keep focus on a subject. Photographic Styles get some additional upgrades and controls, and Time-Lapse also supports 4K. With the 18 Pro, Apple is rolling out a "reference" feature to ensure that an original shot can be confirmed if an edit is later made with AI. Apple calls this a "digital negative." iPhone 18 Pro: ColorsAs previously mentioned, the iPhone 18 Pro's colors may be one of the most recognisably "new" features of this generation. Apple is rolling out color options in "Burgundy," "Glacier," and Silver, though the first two may be the more distinct of the bunch. Still, it's more variation than we have on the Duo.iPhone 18 Pro: PriceEverything is getting more expensive, thanks to RAMaggedon, and the iPhone 18 Pro is no exception. Apple is raising the starting price this year to $1,199 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for the 256GB variant. iPhone 18 Pro: Release dateApple says the iPhone 18 Pro will be available to preorder on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12 a.m. PT (3 a.m. ET). The devices then go on sale Friday, Sept. 18.

title: TikTok Just Announced These Four New Features for Comments
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            TikTok announced four new features coming to its comment section over the next month.
                                            Next month, the app will roll out voice comments, which will let users record and post audio up to 60 seconds.
                                            Creators can add polls to their comment sections to invite viewers to vote on up to five options at a time.
                                            Finally, TikTok is rolling out photo carousel and Live Photos comments as well.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TikTok is famous for its addictive algorithm. And while the videos are certainly the app's main focus, I find the most entertainment in the comments. TikTok commenters can be hilarious, especially since they can use both text and photos to make their jokes. Social media comments are often vile, and while TikTok isn't immune to trolls and their ilk, its comments are generally something else. Now, the comments are changing. On Thursday, TikTok announced four new features that will make comments more visual, interactive, and, well, loud. Not all of these features are out quite yet, but by next month, you might not recognize TikTok's comment section. Text and photo comments aren't going anywhere, but you may find that the comment section is about to get a bit louder. Starting next month, TikTok will support voice comments up to 60 seconds long, which adds a wholly unique type of comment to the mix. Based on TikTok's press release, you can still attach a text-based comment to your voice comment, similar to how photo comments work.While friends may post voice comments on each other's videos à la voice memos in a group chat, I'm guessing that commenters in general will use this feature in ways TikTok doesn't necessarily intend. In fact, this may birth a new type of meme, where users spam videos with obnoxious sound effects and reaction sounds. Think the sounds added to meme edits of viral videos, but in comment form. It's going to be messy, and, likely, hysterical.   
Starting this week, you may see a new interactive element to TikTok comments: polls. TikTok says creators can add polls to the comments of their videos, with up to five voting options per poll. Rather than ask for opinions in the comments, creators can use a poll instead. Creators can choose how long voting lasts, and watch votes appear in real time. It's a small change, but one that could be useful to both big and small creators looking for input from their viewers. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You're no longer limited to posting static images in TikTok's comments. TikTok now supports uploading Live Photos to comments, which should also prove interesting. I could see people thinking they're posting a standard image, but accidentally uploading a Live Photo instead. But seeing as users already know how to add GIFs to comments, I'm not sure how many will want to upload Live Photos. This one might be reserved more for friends commenting on friends' videos, but we'll have to see how users react to know for sure. This last update is perhaps a bit more useful than Live Photo comments. TikTok says it's working on allowing users to upload up to nine photos in one comment, which means the comments section may be literally full of pictures once this launches en masse.  Like standard carousels, users will be able to swipe through your photo uploads, including in a full-screen view. This one will roll out over the course of this month.
